title: Paulson favours further tightening, with room to move gradually
summary: Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson read the October rate hold as a choice about pace. She had supported both September’s increase and October’s hold, and believed more restraint would probably be needed. Gradual moves give households, banks and firms time to adjust loan pricing, funding costs and spending plans. They also let policymakers learn how a volatile equity or oil market is transmitting into demand. Faster action would be warranted if underlying inflation strengthened, wage pressure spread or inflation expectations moved up. She saw little evidence of those particular triggers at the time. These were her preferences, with no exact December move specified.

Paulson compared current conditions with forecasts from the previous December. The median FOMC participant had projected 2.3 percent growth for 2026, year-end unemployment of 4.4 percent and inflation of 2.4 percent. Growth had averaged 2.7 percent so far, October unemployment was 4.1 percent and September twelve-month PCE inflation was 3.6 percent. This comparison shows why she judged demand stronger and inflation more persistent than expected. The dates and horizons differ, so it does not yet score the completed annual forecasts.

The strength extended beyond major technology companies. Every responding firm in the Philadelphia Fed’s October manufacturing survey planned to hold capital spending steady or raise it in the following year. Paulson cited only 20 months since 1968 with that outcome, ten of them in the preceding year. That statistic counts respondents and intentions. It gives neither the magnitude of planned spending nor subsequent investment across the national economy. Real consumption growth had averaged 2.8 percent while real income grew only 1.3 percent. She identified borrowing, lower saving and spending out of investment gains as plausible explanations. A reversal in wealth could make spending less resilient than the recent growth rate suggested.

Average payroll gains in 2026 stood at 86,000 per month against about 10,000 in 2025, with growth across more industries. Wage growth of around 3 percent remained below inflation. Paulson regarded wage pressure as limited despite isolated reports of employers considering cost-of-living increases. The October CPI release, already available when she spoke, reinforced the concern that price pressure persisted. She judged tariff effects on inflation to be fading, while energy and AI-related input costs remained uncertain. Underlying inflation measures clustered between 2.5 and 3 percent and showed little improvement. Her attention to the underlying measures was a way to evaluate the future path of headline inflation, which remained the relevant objective.

Gradual tightening also depended on clear communication. When markets already expect further restraint, anticipated policy can affect financial conditions before the next vote. If that expectation changes, the case for moving slowly can change with it. The speech identifies a conditional strategy, not the realised effect of the speech on prices.

questions.question: How far was the gap between spending and real income being financed by wealth or credit?
questions.detail: Compare saving, borrowing and consumption changes by income and asset ownership, particularly around equity-market swings. Distinguish sustained growth in expected income from one-off withdrawals or unsustainable increases in debt.

questions.question: Were regional capital-spending intentions realised at scale?
questions.detail: Compare the survey’s directional responses with actual spending, order books and project completions by size and sector. A universal intention to maintain or increase expenditure can coexist with small increases in total spending.

questions.question: What evidence would justify moving faster than gradually?
questions.detail: Construct comparable near-term indicators of price breadth, survey expectations, market compensation and wage agreements. Check whether local reports of larger pay settlements spread to a wide set of firms before reading them as a general wage-price mechanism.

questions.question: How much policy news was already in market rates?
questions.detail: Separate the earlier CPI release from Paulson’s evening remarks and other same-day speakers. Compare contracts for specific meetings with their pre-event distributions, and allow for normal overnight liquidity differences.
